subject: Physics
central_question: How are nuclei composed, sized, bound and transformed, and why do radioactive decay, fission and fusion release nuclear energy?
in_scope_units: Introduction to the nucleus as the tiny, positively charged centre containing more than 99.9% of an atom’s mass.
Atomic masses, the atomic mass unit, isotopic abundance and the composition of nuclei in terms of protons and neutrons.
Discovery of the neutron, nuclide notation, atomic number, neutron number, mass number, isotopes, isobars and isotones.
Size of the nucleus, the relation R = R₀A^(1/3), scattering measurements and the near constancy of nuclear density.
Mass defect, nuclear binding energy, binding energy per nucleon and the binding-energy curve.
Properties of the short-range, strong and approximately charge-independent nuclear force.
Radioactivity and the three natural decay modes: alpha, beta and gamma decay.
Nuclear energy and Q-value as consequences of differences in total binding energy and mass.
Nuclear fission of heavy nuclei and its energy release.
Nuclear fusion, the Coulomb barrier and energy generation in stars through the proton–proton cycle.
Controlled thermonuclear fusion, high-temperature plasma and the challenge of confinement.
banned_topics: Rutherford’s full atomic model and Bohr energy levels, which belong to the preceding chapter on atoms.
Detailed exponential radioactive-decay law, decay constant calculations and half-life derivations not developed in the supplied chapter text.
Semiconductor devices and electronic circuits, which belong to Chapter 14.

known_pitfalls.claim: The mass of a nucleus is exactly the sum of the separate masses of its protons and neutrons.
known_pitfalls.correction: A bound nucleus has a smaller mass; the difference is the mass defect whose energy equivalent is the binding energy.

known_pitfalls.claim: All nuclei have the same radius because nuclear density is nearly constant.
known_pitfalls.correction: The radius increases as A^(1/3); constant density follows because nuclear volume is proportional to A.

known_pitfalls.claim: Nuclear force is a long-range inverse-square force like electrostatic force.
known_pitfalls.correction: Nuclear force is very strong but short-ranged, falls rapidly beyond a few femtometres and has no simple law like Coulomb’s law.

known_pitfalls.claim: Fusion starts easily whenever two light nuclei collide.
known_pitfalls.correction: Positively charged nuclei must first overcome the Coulomb barrier and approach closely enough for the short-range nuclear force to act.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Example 13.1 to calculate nuclear density and connect R = R₀A^(1/3) with density independent of mass number.
Use NCERT Example 13.3 to convert one atomic mass unit to 931.5 MeV/c² and interpret the mass defect of oxygen-16.
Apply the Q-value method in NCERT Exercise 13.5 to classify reactions as exothermic or endothermic.
Use NCERT Exercise 13.7 to scale energy released per plutonium fission to all atoms in one kilogram.
Finish with NCERT Example 13.4 to explain conservation and mass–energy interconversion in nuclear and chemical reactions.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter EXERCISES are numbered 13.1 to 13.10 and cover binding energy, nuclear radii, Q-values, fission, fusion and nuclear density.
